title: Did My Husband Fall in Love with Someone Else While Resurrecting Me?
author: Running Peach
synopsis:
Mu Ran had a nightmare. She was a supporting female character in a male-oriented novel, and also the 'white moonlight' wife of the male lead.
In the second year of their marriage, she would die saving him.
To resurrect her, he traveled from the highest heavens to the deepest hells, seeking countless rare treasures. Five hundred years later, he finally tore through the void, reached the pinnacle of cultivation, and successfully brought her back to life.
It sounds like a happy ending, but this is a male-oriented novel.
During the five hundred years the male lead spent trying to save his wife, he encountered countless beauties. Among them, the eldest daughter of the noble Qingtian Sect fell deeply in love with him. When her entire sect besieged him, she even threatened her father with her own life to force him to hand over the treasure needed to resurrect the wife.
The cold-hearted male lead eventually fell for her.
After his wife was resurrected, he gave the young lady a title, and from then on, the three of them lived happily together.
Mu Ran was so infuriated that she sat up in her coffin.
——
Cang Shubai lost his parents at a young age. With mediocre talent and rejected by his family, he did not experience much warmth in his life. His path of cultivation was exceptionally difficult, which naturally forged his decisive, cold, and ruthless personality.
Marrying a young female cultivator was an accident.
He had thought that their stable life of working at sunrise, resting at sunset, and tending to the mundane chores would continue forever, but a siege changed everything.
His wife died for him.
Yet, he insisted on bringing her back to life.
Five hundred years passed; her body gradually regained its warmth, and her soul was about to return.
After finishing a bloody massacre at a forced-marriage scene, Cang Shubai rushed to Linglong Sea. On the water, the person in the white jade coffin was gone, leaving only a letter behind.
—— 'Let us divorce.'"

chapters.title: A Peaceful and Happy Day
chapters.content:
Mu Ran lay in bed, eyes tightly shut, brows furrowed, her hands unconsciously clutching the quilt.

She was trapped deep within a nightmare, unable to escape.

In the dream, she saw many cultivators wielding magical treasures and weapons, shouting things like, "Kill this little demon!"

Her husband was severely wounded. Just as a long sword was about to pierce his chest, she threw herself in front of him to block the blade, dying a gruesome death.

"Husband, you must live on."

With these final words, she breathed her last.

In his grief, her husband tore off his own arm, invoked a forbidden technique, and managed to preserve a tiny fragment of her soul before it dissipated into the heavens and earth.

Amidst a mountain of corpses and a sea of blood, the blood-stained man held her cold body, his eyes lowered as he whispered softly, "I will not let you leave me."

For some reason, the pain in the dream felt exceptionally intense. Mu Ran suddenly opened her eyes and sat up in bed. She panted for a long while before realizing she was covered in a layer of cold sweat.

The moment she woke, the details of the dream began to blur, but she knew she had had a nightmare, and she still remembered the lingering palpitations in her soul.

Flustered, Mu Ran reached for a silver bell placed on the bedside table. Regardless of the fact that it was the middle of the night, she channeled a faint trace of spiritual energy into it. The bell glowed with a silvery light, and soon, a familiar voice came through.

"Ranran, what's wrong?"

Mu Ran sniffled, her voice low and hoarse, "I had a nightmare."

"Don't be afraid; dreams are the opposite of reality."

In the candlelit room, Mu Ran curled her body into a ball, looking quite pitiful.

When she was young, she had the misfortune of being captured by a demonic cultivator to be used for alchemy. Fortunately, her savior arrived in time, and she wasn't thrown into the furnace to become a pill, but she did suffer a head injury that caused her to lose some of her memories.

Ever since then, she had developed a fear of the dark and required a small lamp to be lit at night.

Cang Shubai had specifically stayed with her until she fell asleep before heading out to attend to business. He hadn't expected her to wake up in the middle of the night. Fortunately, Mu Ran often had whimsical ideas and liked to tinker with little gadgets when she was bored.

This communication bell was something she had made; she had one, and Cang Shubai had one, making it quite convenient to stay in touch.

Mu Ran hugged her knees, staring at the small bell, her tone clinging, "Jinzhi, when will you be done and back?"

Jinzhi was Cang Shubai’s courtesy name.

Cang Shubai replied, "Soon."

Mu Ran and Cang Shubai were both low-level cultivators. Mu Ran occasionally took jobs at the town workshops, while Cang Shubai was a doctor at the local clinic, sometimes needing to go up the mountain in the middle of the night to gather herbs.

On the other side of the bell, there was a faint, muffled "woo-woo" sound.

Mu Ran asked with concern, "Jinzhi, are you doing alright over there? You didn't run into any demonic beasts, did you?"

"I'm fine, don't worry."

"I think I heard someone else's voice on your end."

"It’s just Boss Hu talking. We found a decent herb, and he’s quite pleased with it."

Mu Ran muttered, "Alright. It's so dark outside, and I heard there are demonic cultivators killing people lately. You must be careful."

He chuckled softly, "Mm. If you're scared, take out the talismans I left in the cabinet and use them."

"No way, those talismans are so expensive. I have to save them for a critical moment."

After Mu Ran left her family, they had no family support and naturally didn't have much money. She didn't know where Cang Shubai had bought a pile of top-tier life-saving talismans, so she was naturally reluctant to use them unless it was a matter of life and death.

Mu Ran feigned a relaxed tone and said, "Alright, I'm fine now. You're right, dreams are the opposite of reality. I'm not scared. Jinzhi, I'm going back to sleep. Be careful out there."

Cang Shubai said warmly, "Alright."

The bell returned to its dim, lusterless state. Mu Ran put it back, only to hear the sound of wind outside the window. Tree branches struck the glass, making quite a racket.

The shadows of the trees swayed like the claws of a wild beast.

Mu Ran pulled the quilt over her head, shivering.

In the mansion at night, the wind howled.

Amidst the mountain of corpses and sea of blood, the wind, thick with the scent of iron, scattered a pervasive chill. Frost spread rapidly, freezing everything in its path.

The man in green held the now-silent bell in his hand, the warmth in his eyes slowly fading.

He stepped on the remains of an unrecognizable corpse that had turned into an ice sculpture. Lowering his dark red eyes, he looked at the middle-aged man in front of him, whose leg bone was shattered, and asked calmly, "Where is the Hongmeng Glazed Lamp?"

The middle-aged man endured the pain and said, "The Hongmeng Glazed Lamp is the supreme treasure of the Cangshu family! How could it be handed over to a demon who betrayed his clan!"

Suddenly, the corpse under his foot shattered, turning into ice mist and vanishing completely.

"Eldest son!" The middle-aged man watched as his eldest son’s remains were obliterated, his heart filled with grief and indignation.

In just a short time, the Cangshu family had become a mountain of corpses and a sea of blood. No one had expected that the "waste" they once treated as trash, someone they could bully at will, would one day return.

Over the years, no one knew what kind of fortune he had stumbled upon, but his strength had reached a terrifying level. Perhaps only the ancestors of the main family could suppress him.

The world of cultivation was a place where the strong preyed on the weak. If one's strength was inferior to others, sects and families could be wiped out overnight.

"I will ask one more time: where is the Hongmeng Glazed Lamp?"

At this moment, another young man lying on the ground cried out. It turned out one of his arms had been severed, and the wound was bleeding profusely.

The middle-aged man screamed, "Second son!"

That foot stepped onto the second son's head. The second son's face rubbed against the ground, and soon half his face was a bloody mess.

"You should know that I am in a hurry to get home. My patience is limited."

The middle-aged man said, "Cang Shubai, you are also a member of the Cangshu family! Why must you kill us all?"

"Is that so?" Cang Shubai’s expression was indifferent. "When my parents were backlashed by the demonic beasts they raised for the Cangshu family and needed spirit stones for treatment, did the Cangshu family contribute even a single cent? When my mother was critically ill, she knelt and begged you to take me in for the sake of our shared bloodline. You did take me in, but only to use me as fodder for the beasts."

Cang Shubai continued, "Back then, my skills were inferior, so it was only right that I was bullied. Now that I have the strength to make you pay your debts in blood, it is only right that you endure it."

The middle-aged man was Cangshu Yuan, the head of the Cangshu family. Once, he had been so glorious; a single word from him could decide the life or death of a "useless person" in the clan. He never imagined that one day, the person he viewed as "trash" would bring about the destruction of his family.

The second son lay on the ground, weeping bitterly, "Father, save me..."

With corpses piled like mountains all around, Cangshu Yuan was now left with only his second son as his last remaining bloodline.

Cangshu Yuan knew he was doomed. Gritting his teeth, he said, "I can give you the Hongmeng Glazed Lamp, but you must promise to spare my second son!"

Cang Shubai lifted his foot and said, "Very well."

The second son let out a sigh of relief.

Cangshu Yuan sacrificed his soul and summoned a snow-white lotus lamp. Before he died, he said, "Cang Shubai, with the myriad gods as my witness, you promised to spare my second son. You must not... break your word..."

His body collapsed, his eyes wide open, and he ceased to breathe.

The lamp emitted a soft glow. Wherever its light touched, evil spirits were dispelled. Moreover, the lamp's greatest function was to nourish the soul and help stabilize one's foundation. With the Glazed Lamp, cultivation time could be halved, and breakthroughs would become effortless.

The second son shot a hateful glare at the man in green robes before scrambling up from the ground and fleeing into the distance.

Cang Shubai looked down at the lamp in his hand, feeling satisfied. Then, he raised his eyes slightly.

A chilling coldness, like a swimming fish, suddenly emerged, silently drilling into the second son's skin and freezing his blood and bones.

The second son’s running steps froze mid-stride. Before a scream could even escape his throat, he turned into an ice sculpture covered in white frost. He struggled to say, "Cang Shubai... you... you broke your word..."

"I did promise to spare you, but I didn't promise that other things would spare you."

The fish made of frost and snow swam back and disappeared into its master's sleeve.

Cang Shubai turned around. The night wind was desolate and cold, his robes fluttering. The blue-black ends of his hair swayed with his gait, outlining his broad shoulders and narrow waist—like a clear breeze and a bright moon, visible but unreachable.

A faint "crack" sounded. The person turned into an ice sculpture began to shatter inch by inch from his fingertips, eventually scattering into cold powder on the ground, vanishing with a gust of wind.

The wind slipped through a crack in the window and blew out the candle.

Mu Ran lay on the bed, wrapped in her quilt, curled into a ball, her eyes wide and miserable, unable to fall asleep.

She quietly opened a slit in the quilt. It was pitch black, and her heart sank further. She debated whether to get out of bed to light the lamp.

Suddenly, light spilled into the room once more.

Mu Ran was scooped up, quilt and all.

"I'm back."

It was the familiar voice.

Mu Ran poked her head out of the quilt. Seeing the familiar face, her eyes curved into a smile, bright and beaming, "Jinzhi!"

Reassured, she crawled out of the quilt, opened her arms, and threw herself into his embrace.

Cang Shubai was much taller than her. As he lowered his hands to pat her back, he almost completely encircled her in his arms, shielding her from the midnight chill.

"The wind is a bit strong tonight. I'm sorry, I shouldn't have gone out this evening."

Mu Ran shook her head, lifting her face with sparkling eyes, "Jinzhi went out to earn money to support the family. I understand. It's not your fault; it's just that I'm a coward, and I couldn't help but disturb you while you were busy."

"It's not a disturbance." He lifted her chin and pressed a gentle kiss to the corner of her lips. Reluctant to pull away, he murmured against her lips, "No matter when it is, I am always happy when you come to me."

Mu Ran wrapped her arms around his neck. Her long hair cascaded down. Even without makeup, her smile was as bright and brilliant as ever when she looked at him.

Cang Shubai couldn't help but let his own lips curve upward. He stroked her long hair, the soft touch feeling as if he were brushing against the clouds.

Mu Ran noticed a new glazed lamp on the table. She pursed her lips and said, "You bought something useless again."

"I bought this lamp from a traveling merchant. It has a spell cast on it; it can be brightened or extinguished according to the owner's will."

Isn't that just like a voice-activated light?

Huh?

Mu Ran frowned slightly. What is a voice-activated light? Why did she think of such a strange term?

She snapped out of it and took Cang Shubai's hand, "But this must have been very expensive."

Cang Shubai shook his head, "It's just a lamp that stays lit a little longer than ordinary ones. It doesn't have much use; it only cost half a spirit stone."

Mu Ran climbed up, grabbed her coin purse, and opened his large hand, placing five spirit stones into his palm.

"You're always buying things for the house; your pocket money must be running low. If you go out to socialize, you can't be without money for food—it would be embarrassing."

Cang Shubai chuckled, "Mm, thank you for your generosity, my wife."

The family's finances were in her hands. Cang Shubai never kept private funds; whatever he earned, he handed over.

Mu Ran leaned into his embrace and covered her mouth with a yawn.

Cang Shubai took off his outer robes and lay down with her. As soon as the quilt was pulled over them, she naturally snuggled into his arms.

"Jinzhi, goodnight."

Cang Shubai lowered his head and kissed the top of her hair, "Goodnight."

Mu Ran closed her eyes contentedly and drifted into a beautiful dream.

How wonderful. Today was another peaceful and happy day.

chapters.title: Seventy Percent Full
chapters.content:
It was late autumn, and as the days grew colder, lazy people only wanted to curl up in their quilts and refuse to get out of bed.

However, the aroma of food kept drifting into her nose, enticing the person still sleeping to open her eyes.

Following the scent, Mu Ran sat up in bed, dazed and groggy. She recognized the scent of breakfast as her favorite seven-treasure porridge.

She instantly felt energized. She quickly put on her clothes, stepped into her shoes, ran out of the room, crossed the main hall, and dashed into the kitchen.

The morning light spilled over the kitchen window lattice, landing on the plain cyan robe the man was wearing, making his refined temperament seem almost ethereal, as if he were not a mortal.

The man had his sleeves rolled up to his forearms, revealing a red string tied around his wrist. He lowered his eyes as he held a porcelain spoon to taste the porridge. Even the way his hem hung, accentuating his tall and relaxed posture, added a touch of worldly warmth to him.

Cang Shubai added a bit more sugar to the porridge. Hearing the stealthy footsteps, he acted as if he hadn't heard anything. Sure enough, not long after, someone hugged him from behind.

Mu Ran poked her head out from behind him. "You worked hard going out in the middle of the night. We agreed that I would make breakfast today."

Cang Shubai looked back. "Then I’ll have to eat breakfast and lunch together."

He was teasing her for waking up late.

Mu Ran pressed her face against his back, muttering unconvinced, "Actually, I woke up a long time ago, but seeing that you got up so early, I decided to sleep a little longer on your behalf."

"Then, will you also eat a little more on my behalf in a moment?"

Mu Ran raised her face and laughed. "That’s not impossible."

Cang Shubai held her hand, his gaze gentle. "Go wash up; the porridge will be ready soon."

Mu Ran nodded obediently. She went to wash up, then sat before the vanity to comb her hair in front of the mirror.

The person in the mirror still had eyes moist from sleep, sparkling as if they held light. Her black hair was braided into a pretty style with a green hair tie, perfectly matching the light green ru skirt she was wearing today.

Cang Shubai walked past the door carrying a bowl of porridge. Catching a glimpse of her tucking away loose strands of hair in the mirror, he set the bowl down and walked over. He reached out and gently tucked that strand of hair hanging by her cheek behind her ear, his fingertips inadvertently brushing against the tip of her ear. "If you dawdle any longer, the porridge will get cold."

In the mirror, his brows and eyes were curved, and even the arc of his cyan robe hem sweeping across her chair back carried a hint of warmth.

Mu Ran finally pinned a pearl flower into her hair and happily followed him out of the room.

But she couldn't sit still. It just so happened that the sun was shining brightly today. By the time Cang Shubai finished cleaning the kitchen and came out, Mu Ran had already taken her bowl out of the house to chat with the neighbor aunts from the village.

The neighbor aunt’s surname was Wang, and everyone called her Aunt Wang. She usually took on some laundry work, and sometimes when she couldn't finish it, she would distribute the work to other aunts, so her house could be considered a small hub for gossip.

Aunt Wang said mysteriously, "Hey, have you heard? The couple at the Li family at the entrance of the village had a terrible fight a few nights ago."

The other aunts were curious as they worked. "What happened?"

Mu Ran sat on a small stool and nodded along. "What happened?"

Aunt Wang lowered her voice. "It’s all because of the Li family’s daughter-in-law being pregnant."

"Pregnancy is a good thing."

Mu Ran chimed in, "Yeah, it’s a good thing."

Aunt Wang glanced at the others. "But the problem is, Li Ergou has been away selling goods for three months, yet his wife has been pregnant for a month."

"Oh my, that’s truly a sin!"

Mu Ran took a spoonful of porridge and chewed the lotus seeds inside with relish. "Such a sin."

One aunt said, "Every time I pass by the entrance of the village, the dog they keep barks at me, but when the village butcher, Fan, passes by, the dog doesn't make a sound. The butcher and the Li family's dog are so familiar—there must be something wrong!"

"That's right, you really shouldn't say that, but maybe the one who cuckolded Li Ergou really is the butcher!"

"Li Ergou was crying and howling, saying he wanted to throw himself into the river."

"He's an honest man; there's no need to go to such extremes!"

Mu Ran swallowed a mouthful of porridge and chimed in, "Isn't that so? Even if the child isn't his, the wife is at least his."

The aunts all looked at Mu Ran in unison, their expressions somewhat strange.

When a group of women gathered to gossip, the young wives in the village would feel intimidated, but Mu Ran was quite an outlier; she always had to join in the fun.

However, Mu Ran had one advantage: she was very cooperative. Regardless of whether she had anything to say, she would always respond and never let the conversation die. They actually quite liked this young wife.

Aunt Wang kindly reminded her, "Xiao Ran, don't you often go to town to take on work? And your man, he goes to work at the medical clinic in town every day. You two must be careful. I heard from my husband that some demonic cultivators are killing people indiscriminately, and the town is now under martial law."

Mu Ran’s expression changed. "That’s terrifying!"

Strictly speaking, the law of the jungle was the norm in the cultivation world. To become stronger, no one’s hands were entirely clean. There were thousands of paths to cultivation, and among them, there were those who cultivated through "slaughter." Since incidents of killing people for treasures happened often, such people were naturally called demonic cultivators.

Mu Ran had some cultivation, but not much. That was why, after leaving her family, she and Cang Shubai, who also had mediocre cultivation, chose to settle in a small village far from conflict.

Aunt Wang said, "In my opinion, you’d better quit your jobs in town."

Another aunt said, "You’re advising Xiao Ran not to go to town, but isn't your own husband still running errands in town?"

Aunt Wang waved her hand, saying helplessly, "If it weren't for the debts our family owed to treat my illness years ago, I really wouldn't want him to run errands in town. Plain tea and rice every day would be just fine."

Mu Ran finished her bowl of porridge. When she was about to return, Aunt Wang pulled her aside and whispered to her alone:

"I heard from my husband that the wealthy Mr. Chen in town has been specifically asking whether the young man at the medical clinic has a family. You should be careful; your man is so alluring, watch out for someone snatching him away."

Mu Ran had never heard Cang Shubai mention anything about Mr. Chen. She nodded, thanked Aunt Wang, and ran back with light steps, holding the empty bowl.

One aunt sighed, "This little girl really has a good life, being waited on hand and foot. Why don't I have such good luck to find a husband who knows how to cherish someone so well?"

Aunt Wang sneered, "Then you should have grown up as pretty as this little girl first."

Mu Ran passed through the fence gate. As she neared the door of the main hall, she stopped.

Cang Shubai was sitting on a wooden chair in the hall. His posture was upright yet not stiff. The hem of his plain cyan robe draped over the edge of the chair, making the white porcelain porridge bowl he held between his fingertips look even more refined.

The morning light fell on his profile, but it seemed to be blocked out by a faint sense of detachment. Even the way he drank his porridge was so elegant that it made people afraid to approach him easily.

However, when he raised his eyes and her figure fell into his dark pupils, the corners of his eyes curved slightly, and the detachment transformed into tenderness.

Mu Ran stood at the doorway, pacing left and right, shaking her head, occasionally touching her chin, frowning, and staring at him incessantly.

Cang Shubai asked softly, "What are you doing?"

Mu Ran kept a straight face. "Don't disturb me, I'm thinking seriously."

Cang Shubai put down the bowl in his hand and truly stopped talking, his expression relaxed, letting her examine him.

After a long while, Mu Ran finally confirmed something. She said, "My husband is indeed good-looking!"

Cang Shubai’s eyes flickered, and he reached out toward her.

Mu Ran stepped up the stairs, entered the main door, and reached his side. Her hand was held by his, and the empty bowl in her other hand was taken and set aside by him. At the same time, he pulled her to sit beside him.

He didn't speak, only raised his hand to gently touch the green hair tie in her hair, and then smoothed the loose strands by her ears that had become messy from running. His fingertips lingered on her ear and did not leave.

"Jinzhi, that tickles."

She couldn't stand it and wanted to dodge to the side, but she didn't know how he was applying force; she didn't feel any pain, yet she couldn't break free from his restraint. She could only remain circled within the space filled with his scent.

He asked, "Are you full?"

Mu Ran shook her head. "I only drank one bowl of porridge, I’m only seventy percent full. I want to drink another bowl."

"No rush."

Mu Ran tilted her head. "Why no rush?"

A pair of hands gripped her waist. Her body suddenly lifted into the air, and she was picked up. In her panic, she wrapped her hands and feet around him, like a koala clinging to him.

Cang Shubai supported her buttocks with one hand, turned around easily, stroked the hair at the back of her head, and kissed the corner of her lips. "Let's go take care of other things first. I'll make you something delicious at noon."

They entered the bedroom. A gust of wind blew, and the door closed, shutting out the morning light.

Before long, soft, fragmented voices echoed in the dim environment.

"What delicious thing are you going to make for me?"

"What do you want to eat?"

"I heard... I heard that Eight-Color Braised Delicacies is very delicious. Many top-tier cultivators might not even get to eat it, especially one of the ingredients, which requires the meat of a Fire Qilin Beast. It’s very dangerous and hard to find."

"Alright, tomorrow I will go and raid the Fire Qilin Beast's nest."

"You really know how to joke..." Her voice suddenly changed pitch. "Jinzhi!"

"Hmm?"

"Gently, a little more gently!"

"You just said you were seventy percent full, I can't be gentle."

"..."

chapters.title: Chapter 3 I’ll Help You
chapters.content:
Cang Shubai had accompanied Dr. Hu to the mountains to gather herbs the previous night, so he was able to head to the medical clinic in town after lunch the next day.

As usual, he ate lunch with Mu Ran, tidied up the dishes, and prepared to leave.

When he reached the front gate, he turned back.

Mu Ran, having eaten her fill, was sitting in a chair with her hands resting on the table, supporting her chin. Her eyes were closed, and her head swayed back and forth; she looked drowsy, very cozy and comfortable.

Cang Shubai said, "I’m leaving now."

Mu Ran opened her eyes a crack. "Oh, go ahead."

Cang Shubai turned around, then said again, "Ranran."

"Hmm?"

"I’m leaving now."

Mu Ran stared at him blankly for a good while before she suddenly realized what he meant. She hopped off the chair, hurried over to him, hugged him, and patted his back gently.

"Jinzhi, be careful on your way. I’ll wait for you to come home."

Cang Shubai leaned down, resting his chin on the top of her head. His fingertips brushed against her green hair ribbon, and his lips curved slightly. "Wait for me to come back and make dinner."

Mu Ran gave two obedient "mm-hmms," then stood on tiptoe and kissed his chin. "Go quickly, don't be late, or the boss will dock your pay again."

He ruffled her hair and chuckled.

Not long after Cang Shubai left, Mu Ran tidied herself up and hurried out as well.

Auntie Wang was hanging up laundry and, seeing Mu Ran emerge from the neighboring courtyard, she remarked, "Xiao Ran, are you heading to town for work again?"

Mu Ran nodded and shook the toolbox slung over her left shoulder. "I promised the workshop owner I’d go help out today."

Auntie Wang said, "Your husband earns a decent living, why do you always have to go to town and tire yourself out?"

"Didn't you say it yourself, Auntie Wang? Things haven't been peaceful lately. I want to earn some extra money, and then I’ll find a chance to tell Jinzhi I’m quitting the job in town. By the way, Auntie Wang, please..."

Auntie Wang replied, "I know, I’ll just pretend I didn't see anything and won't say a word to your man."

Mu Ran grinned and waved. "Thanks, Auntie Wang! I’m off!"

Watching Mu Ran’s retreating figure, Auntie Wang couldn't help but smile and sigh, "Those two really are like a celestial couple; they are so deeply in love."

In the past, if Mu Ran needed to travel far, she would have used a flight talisman to reach her destination at high speed. But she had to save money now, and she couldn't bear to buy such things.

It took her over an hour to walk to town, which was bustling with people coming and going.

Perhaps what Auntie Wang said about the demonic cultivators becoming more rampant lately was true; at the very least, she saw far more cultivators on the street than before, creating a tense atmosphere as if a storm were brewing.

Mu Ran withdrew her gaze and entered the Song family workshop.

Boss Song was over fifty but still full of energy. He had been listlessly leaning on the counter, fiddling with an abacus, but his eyes lit up when he saw Mu Ran. "Oh, my dear Miss Mu, you’ve finally arrived."

There happened to be some customers browsing in the shop, and when they heard "Miss Mu," two men looked over in unison.

Mu Ran quickly said, "Boss Song, I’m just a village woman, please don't call me that every time! I can't handle it!"

The two men, who were traveling together, looked at each other and whispered.

"I thought she was actually the young lady from Biyun Mountain."

"That young lady was stripped of her cultivation, removed from the family register, and driven off the mountain three years ago because she refused to marry the Young Palace Master of the Wuyu Palace. If she’s still alive, she must be in a sorry state."

"That’s true. I heard the second Miss Mu married in her place. If she knew that the Young Palace Master, who was once a comatose waste, had awakened and even inherited the position of Palace Master, she would surely die of regret."

Having been cast out of the Mu clan of Biyun Mountain, a lone woman surely wouldn't fare well in this world where the strong prey on the weak.

The woman carving wood in the workshop before them was exceptionally bright and beautiful. Although she was working, her skin was delicate and tender, clearly indicating she had been well-cared for and had never suffered.

How could she be that young lady of the Mu family who had been expelled from her clan and was likely begging for scraps somewhere?

These two cultivators were dressed in fine clothes and looked like strangers; they were likely from out of town and probably hailed from some famous sect.

Usually, such cultivators were arrogant and wouldn't look twice at goods from such a small place.

Boss Song didn't expect them to buy anything, so he chatted idly with Mu Ran, who was carving wood at her workbench.

"The mirror you made last time, the girls in town love it. One look in the mirror and they can... can..."

Mu Ran said, "Beautify."

"Yes, yes, that’s it, 'beautify'." Boss Song clicked his tongue in wonder. "I really don't know where you get so many ideas to make such strange and wonderful things. Oh, by the way, the young lady from the Chen household wants to order a batch of mirrors as gifts."

Mu Ran nodded. "As long as the pay is good, I’ll make as many as you need."

A smile appeared on Boss Song’s face. "Dr. Cang is truly blessed to have a wife as clever and capable as you."

Mu Ran smiled. "I think it’s my blessing to have such a good husband."

Come to think of it, there was no soul-stirring story behind how Mu Ran and Cang Shubai met.

At that time, she needed a place to stay and didn't want to attract attention, and she had to save her spirit stones, so she rented a small courtyard in the quiet outskirts.

Cang Shubai lived across from her then. Although they were neighbors, over the course of half a year, they only caught glimpses of each other when they occasionally went out, barely nodding acquaintances who didn't even know each other's names.

Their true fate began on a rainy night.

Mu Ran’s roof leaked badly, and her room was almost completely flooded. Distressed for her furniture, she had no choice but to hold an umbrella and knock on the door across the way.

The door opened to reveal a young gentleman in green robes, his dark hair unbound. "Is something the matter?"

Raindrops rolled down the folds of his green clothing, looking even more refreshing than the curtain of rain falling from the eaves.

She was soaked through and looked quite disheveled. Gathering her courage, she asked softly, "My roof is leaking and needs repairs. Do you happen to have a ladder?"

The gentleman nodded. "I do."

Her eyes lit up. "May I borrow it?"

He said, "The ladder is in the woodshed. I’ll go get it."

The young man in green stood under the eaves, then suddenly looked back at her.

The umbrella she was holding was tilted slightly by the wind, and half of her shoulder was already soaked through. Her light-colored dress clung to her body, making her figure appear even more slender.

Seeming to sense his gaze, she looked up. The rain misted her hair, with a few strands sticking to her fair cheeks, and blurred her dark, glistening eyes.

Later, he said, "I’ll help you."

On that rainy night, they exchanged names. After that, they grew more and more familiar, and half a year later, it was only natural that they got married.

chapters.title: Mung Bean Cake
chapters.content:
Mu Ran lowered her head, focusing on her work. Before long, the piece of wood in her hands had become a small wooden chicken. It looked chubby, but after she infused it with a tiny spirit stone, it actually flapped its wings and flew up.

Boss Song hurried over. "What new gadget are you researching this time?"

Mu Ran reached out her hand. "Boss Song, give me one of your hairs."

Boss Song didn't hesitate to pluck out a hair.

Mu Ran spoke to the little wooden chicken: "Deliver a message for me: Boss Song, it’s time to pay my wages."

A crack opened on the little wooden chicken’s chest. She placed the hair in front of the crack; it was sucked inside, and the seam closed.

The little wooden chicken flapped its wings and flew in front of Boss Song. Its wooden beak opened and closed, emitting a girl’s voice: "Boss Song, it’s time to pay my wages."

Excitement appeared on Boss Song’s face. He circled the little wooden chicken, looking at it from left to right. "Wonderful, simply wonderful! Have you given it a name?"

"It can find someone using a single hair and deliver a message on my behalf. I call it a 'Paging Chicken'."

"Paging Chicken... a good name, truly a good name!"

Two cultivators nearby had already noticed the situation. They walked over together and said with great interest, "How much for this Paging Chicken? We’ll take it."

Although this thing wasn't a magical treasure, its value lay in how interesting it was. Giving it to someone of higher status to amuse them would be a good gesture.

Mu Ran didn't know how to negotiate business. Boss Song gave her a wink, and she sat down to continue carving other wood, appearing as if she were deaf to the world outside her window.

Boss Song smiled. "As you two guests can see, this Paging Chicken is not easy to make. I’m afraid that in this whole world, only our craftsman can produce one. But since we’ve met today, it’s fate. For the sake of this connection, I certainly won't ask for an exorbitant price. How about this: one hundred spirit stones."

The two cultivators exclaimed in surprise, "One hundred spirit stones!?"

Even Mu Ran, who was busy carving, was startled by the figure.

One hundred spirit stones was equivalent to half a year’s worth of expenses for an ordinary person.

She wiped the cold sweat from her forehead, thinking to herself that Boss Song really dared to say anything.

However, after the time it takes to drink a cup of tea, he actually succeeded in closing the deal.

The Paging Chicken was sold for ninety spirit stones. The cultivators were dressed in fine attire, and naturally, they could afford the price if they gritted their teeth. The people they served had seen many precious items, but rarely anything so novel; perhaps buying it wouldn't be a loss after all.

"As we agreed, a three-to-seven split. This is your share." Boss Song gave Mu Ran sixty-three spirit stones and added, "Keep bringing your good work here to sell."

Mu Ran was in a hurry to get back, so she tucked the money away. "Got it, I’m heading back now."

Boss Song watched her running out the door. "Are you coming back tomorrow?"

"We'll see!"

Before long, she had disappeared from sight.

It wasn't dark yet, and the vendors were still out. Mu Ran bought a bag of beef jerky and some mung bean cakes that Cang Shubai liked before heading back. Just as she reached the tree-lined path, a vicious dog blocked her way.

Mu Ran could tell at a glance that this wasn't an ordinary dog, but a spirit pet kept by someone.

It must have been starving, as it drooled while staring at Mu Ran.

Mu Ran slowly took two steps back.

The massive, vicious dog also closed in by two steps.

Mu Ran swallowed nervously, then suddenly tossed the beef jerky in her hand to the side.

The vicious dog immediately pounced on it, opening its blood-red maw to tear into it frantically.

Mu Ran seized the opportunity and ran.

Not long after, a fragrant breeze wafted over.

A woman in red, wearing a veil, had a slender figure and features as delicate as a painting. Her eyes were filled with ripples, beautiful enough to be a celestial being.

A sword-wielding maid glared at the ravenous dog and scolded, "You stupid dog! The Fairy ordered you to fast for three months to cultivate a demonic beast's body. Now that you've eaten, all our efforts have gone to waste!"

Another maid, carrying a green lantern, also said indignantly, "Which blind fool threw food to this stupid dog? Fairy, shall we investigate?"

The woman in red withdrew her indifferent gaze, her voice cold. "The priority is to find the old man 'Long Jian'. Two hundred years ago, he killed people and stole treasure in the Void Secret Realm. That debt must be settled. After all these years, word finally came that he was hiding in this backwater town to heal his wounds. We must not alert the enemy."

Her brow furrowed slightly as she said, "Back then, if a man in green hadn't suddenly interfered, the champion of the secret realm should have been me. I must kill him and that old man Long Jian to wash away my shame!"

The surrounding air suddenly turned cold, and the two maids held their breath, terrified.

Ever since returning from the secret realm two hundred years ago, the Fairy’s state of mind had been compromised, making her breakthroughs exceptionally difficult. That man in green who had suddenly appeared seemed to have left a deep trauma, giving rise to a terrifying obsession.

Mu Ran ran all the way home, but she had miscalculated; Cang Shubai had already returned and finished cooking.

Thinking quickly, she hid her toolbox in a pile of firewood before entering, smoothed her hair, and walked in clutching the pastries.

"Jinzhi, why are you home so early today?"

Cang Shubai was setting the table and looked up at her. "There weren't many patients today, so Dr. Hu let me come home early."

Mu Ran felt a bit guilty but braced herself. She smiled and placed the pastries in his hands. "I went to sit at Auntie Wang's for a while. Look, these are the mung bean cakes I asked her husband to bring from town."

Cang Shubai wasn't in a hurry to eat. He reached out to gently brush a stray hair from her ear and asked in a low voice, "You went to sit at Auntie Wang's, so why are you out of breath?"

Mu Ran’s eyes darted away. "I just... I just had a momentary lack of energy. I get winded after walking a few steps."

"Let me take your pulse."

"No need, I'm hungry! I'm going to wash my hands first!"

Mu Ran hurried into the kitchen to wash her hands, her retreat looking very much like a flight in panic.

Cang Shubai didn't say anything more. He sat in his chair, looking at the mung bean cakes in the paper wrapping—kept perfectly intact—and a warmth returned to his eyes.

A moment later, Mu Ran ran back. She tried hard to control her breathing and smiled at him, finally no longer panting.

Cang Shubai set the pastries aside, picked up a bowl, ladled some meat soup, and placed it in her hands. "I made a new dish today. Taste it and see if you like it."

Mu Ran took a sip, tasting the rich, complex flavors of the ingredients woven together. She said, "It's delicious."

Cang Shubai placed a piece of meat into her bowl. "I'm glad you like it."

Mu Ran asked curiously, "What is this dish called? I haven't seen you make it before."

He said, "Meat soup."

Mu Ran was stunned. "Just 'meat soup'?"

He nodded. "Just meat soup."

Mu Ran didn't know what kind of meat was in the bowl, but it was quite chewy. She sat with poor posture, leaning against him even while eating. "Jinzhi is amazing. Everything you make is delicious."

He always balanced meat and vegetables for her; the most tender heart of a green vegetable went into her bowl. He asked softly, "Tell me next time you want to drink meat soup, and I'll make it for you again."

Mu Ran shook her head. "It's delicious, but I don't think it tastes particularly different from other meat. I still prefer the home-cooked meals you make."

He smiled faintly. "Mm."

Mu Ran’s sharp eyes suddenly caught something, and she grabbed his hand. "Jinzhi, you're hurt."

There was a burn mark on the back of his hand, very conspicuous against his pale skin.

"I accidentally burned myself while decocting medicine. It's nothing serious."

"No, your body belongs to me. I can't bear for you to be hurt. Even if you don't feel pain, my heart aches for you." She hopped off the chair, acting decisively, and rushed toward the bedroom. "We have burn ointment at home; I'll go find it."

Cang Shubai watched her retreating figure, a soft, fragmented tenderness spreading in his eyes.

His fingertips picked up a piece of mung bean cake and he put it in his mouth. As the sweetness melted on his tongue, the corners of his lips curled into a faint arc.

chapters.title: Firefly Light
chapters.content:
“Be smarter when you work in the future. Don’t be so foolish, rushing to do everything yourself.”

Mu Ran carefully applied ointment to his wound. Fearing she might hurt him, she deliberately softened her touch, her nagging never ceasing.

“It’s one thing that you’re always sent out to see difficult patients, but they even make you gather herbs late at night, and you’re the one who has to decoct them. You’re busier than an old ox.”

“I’ve long wanted you to stop working at Dr. Hu’s clinic. You don’t know how to slack off; whatever tasks he assigns, you just go and work yourself to the bone. In the end, you’re the one who suffers.”

“No, that’s not right.” Mu Ran thought of something and looked up at him. “I suffer too. Seeing you hurt makes my heart ache.”

Cang Shubai’s eyes curved slightly at the corners. “It was an accident. It won’t happen again.”

Mu Ran was still unhappy. She held his large hand and examined it closely.

His finger bones were distinct but not sharp, and the joints bore thin calluses—traces left from years of holding a brush or working, which instead added a sense of grounded substance.

On the back of his hand, even the faint path of the veins beneath the skin looked as if they had been meticulously outlined, making his hands appear both powerful and filled with an indescribable gentleness.

Mu Ran muttered, “Jinzhi’s hands are so beautiful; it would be a pity if they were scarred.”

His hand moved. His palm was wide, able to firmly wrap around hers, and his fingers interlaced with hers, locking them together.

Cang Shubai leaned down, bringing his face close to hers, his dark eyes almost entirely filled with her reflection.

“There won’t be any scars. I promise you.”

Mu Ran inexplicably felt that this sounded as if he were promising not to let something he cherished be damaged.

She tilted her head forward, closing the remaining distance between them.

Their nose tips touched, and they could feel each other’s breath.

Mu Ran said softly, “Until your wound heals, you are not allowed to overwork yourself.”

He said, “Okay.”

“If Dr. Hu tries to make things difficult for you again and you feel too embarrassed to speak up, I will go to him myself and tell him you’re quitting.”

He said again, “Okay.”

“I’ll wash the dishes today; you sit and rest.”

A low chuckle rolled from his throat, his warm breath brushing against her nose. “Okay.”

Mu Ran asked, “Can you stop saying ‘okay’ to everything I say?”

Cang Shubai: “Okay.”

Mu Ran glared at him.

His fingertips curled slightly, gently rubbing against the skin of her hand. “I’ll listen to whatever you say.”

Mu Ran let out a soft huff, ignored him, and carried the bowls and chopsticks into the kitchen.

Cang Shubai rested his chin on one hand on the table, his eyes quietly watching her busy figure through the kitchen doorway.

The sunset’s afterglow was warm, wrapping Mu Ran’s busy silhouette in a cozy golden rim.

The water flowed with a "swish" over the porcelain bowls, creating crisp, delicate sounds that, mixed with the occasional breeze outside the window, became the most beautiful music.

Cang Shubai’s deep, dark eyes curved slightly.

So, in these peaceful days, watching the person one loves busy with the mundane chores of life, even time itself seems to slow down.

The scent of blood from his memories was washed away by quite a bit.

Mu Ran suddenly turned back. “Jinzhi, do you want to go for a walk later?”

Cang Shubai replied with the same word: “Okay.”

As expected, she glared at him again.

The world was not peaceful, so walks could only happen before nightfall. The villagers, having nothing else to do, would stroll around not far from their homes.

Mu Ran hid the money she had earned that day in a small box and led Cang Shubai out the door.

“I heard Auntie Wang say there are fern roots on the mountain east of the village. If you grind them into powder, they make delicious rice cakes. If I have time another day, I’ll go join them.”

“And at the entrance of the village, Li Ergou and Butcher Fan got into a fight. Auntie Wang said Li Ergou didn’t win, and now his wife is making a scene, wanting to divorce him to be with Butcher Fan, but Li Ergou won’t agree.”

“Li Ergou went out to earn money to support his family, never expecting his wife to run off with someone else when he returned. Come to think of it, he’s truly pitiful.”

Mu Ran’s mouth never stopped, chattering away like a stream of consciousness, recounting all the messy gossip she had heard from Auntie Wang.

Cang Shubai occasionally chimed in, “Ranran is right.”

The evening glow was perfect, and along the way, they saw men, women, and children from the village out for strolls.

The villagers would always seek Cang Shubai for any aches or pains, and since he never charged for his services, he was well-liked. Everyone they passed would greet them, and inevitably, someone would tease them.

“Dr. Cang and your wife are so affectionate! My spouse and I haven’t held hands on walks since we were married for six months.”

Mu Ran felt a bit embarrassed and tried to pull her hand away, but despite trying again and again, she didn’t succeed.

Cang Shubai was low-key and reserved by nature, yet he seemed to have no awareness of the need to keep a proper distance from her.

Mu Ran whispered, “Let go, people will laugh at us.”

He said, “There are many forks in the village paths. If I let go, I’ll get lost.”

Cang Shubai had always been indifferent toward people and things; it was only after they married that Mu Ran discovered the passion he hid behind his aloofness.

Sometimes he would come out with such nonsense that she still needed time to adjust.

Mu Ran had to move closer to him, acting as if she were burying her head in the sand, thinking that if they were close enough and her sleeves covered their hands, others wouldn’t see they were holding hands.

It was getting late, so they turned back along the path they had come.

Night had just fallen when, unexpectedly, a speck of green light flew past.

Mu Ran exclaimed in surprise, “A firefly!”

Cang Shubai reached out and easily caught the firefly before it could fly away. He then opened his hand in front of her, and a tiny glow flickered in his palm.

Mu Ran hugged his arm and said curiously, “How can there still be fireflies at this time of year?”

Generally, living creatures liked to linger in places rich with spiritual energy, but this small village had none.

Cang Shubai said, “Perhaps it’s a straggler that lost its way.”

He watched her eyes, which were filled with interest, and softened his voice. “Do you like it?”

Mu Ran nodded.

Cang Shubai chuckled. Suddenly, a breeze blew by, his green robes fluttering and outlining his slender, graceful figure.

He said, “Ranran, look.”

Mu Ran turned back.

Specks of firefly light drifted out from the grass. At first, there were only two or three, like fragments of stars that had accidentally fallen from the sky. Gradually, the points of light gathered, more and more, until even the evening breeze seemed wrapped in tiny, shimmering dust.

Mu Ran looked back, her eyes shining as if they held stars, her tone excited. “How can there be so many fireflies!”

The firefly in Cang Shubai’s hand flew away, merging into this dance of starlight.

He held her hand. “Perhaps they found the straggler and all came back to find it.”

Mu Ran smiled brightly. “Its family didn’t abandon it. That’s wonderful.”

Cang Shubai’s gaze rested on her smiling eyes and brows. “Yes, it truly is.”

chapters.title: Silly Goose
chapters.content:
The temperature had fluctuated wildly of late, and the number of patients at the town’s medical clinic had increased accordingly.

"Take one dose of medicine daily, abstain from alcohol and agitation, and pay more attention to rest. You will be well within five days."

Butcher Fan took the medicine with his face bruised and swollen. He tried to smile his thanks, but the movement tugged at the wounds on his face. He gasped in pain and muttered under his breath, "That bastard Li Ergou."

Cang Shubai kept his head down, busy with the ledger, pretending he hadn't heard the butcher’s profanity.

Butcher Fan glanced to the side.

Dr. Hu was a man in his thirties. His thin frame and prominent cheekbones gave him a somewhat mean-spirited appearance. He watched his only shop assistant work with cold eyes, while he himself sat in a rocking chair, peeling melon seeds and swaying back and forth in great comfort.

Butcher Fan whispered, "Little Doctor, with Dr. Hu squeezing you like this, doesn't your beautiful wife feel sorry for you?"

Cang Shubai stopped his brush and lifted his eyes slightly.

Butcher Fan suddenly shivered and shrank his neck.

He was from the same village as Cang Shubai, so he naturally knew about the beautiful young woman in the village. No one knew how she had been raised, but she was so vibrant and spirited; when she curled her eyes and smiled at someone, it felt as if it could melt a person's heart.

It was a pity she already had a husband. Her husband was also quite extraordinary—refined and handsome. The young couple always went out and returned together; they were truly a match made in heaven.

Butcher Fan had self-awareness; he knew that such a beautiful woman would never look his way. He had only spoken out of turn because Cang Shubai always seemed so mild-tempered, and he wanted to tease him a little.

For some reason, Butcher Fan felt a chill run down his spine just from that one glance from Cang Shubai. He swallowed hard. "I have things to do, I'll be going now."

Butcher Fan grabbed his medicine and hurried out.

There were no other outsiders left in the clinic.

Dr. Hu suddenly jumped down from his chair. Carrying the plate of shelled melon seeds, he ran over obsequiously. "Godfather, you rest! Let me handle the work!"

Cang Shubai didn't look up, ignoring the offering. He continued writing his list of medicinal herbs, his tone flat. "I told you, don't call me that."

"There's no one else around, so it's fine for me to call you Godfather!"

The man who had looked so mean-spirited just moments ago was now acting like a sycophant, fawning over him in a way that was quite comical.

Cang Shubai put down his brush and walked out from behind the counter.

"Godfather, don't move. I know you must have finished making the tortoise jelly. I'll go pack it!" Dr. Hu set down the plate of seeds and ran into the courtyard behind the clinic.

Cang Shubai let him be. He sat in a chair, poured a cup of tea, and opened a volume of the *Medical Classics*.

Before long, Dr. Hu ran back out, carefully carrying a bamboo tube filled with tortoise jelly, and set it gently on the table.

"Godfather, this stuff is a nuisance to make, and no one buys it. Why do you always insist on making it?"

"Mixed with milk, Ranran likes it."

Dr. Hu carefully observed Cang Shubai’s expression and muttered under his breath, "Isn't Godfather here to experience a mortal life to break through a cultivation bottleneck? Marriage is one of the most important parts of mortal life, but looking at it now, Godfather, have you really started treating that low-level female cultivator as your wife?"

Cang Shubai said, "She is my wife."

Dr. Hu was stunned for a moment, then put on a flattering smile. "Then in the future, I'll brew more tortoise jelly to give to the Mistress!"

It had to be said that after following Cang Shubai for a hundred years, he had learned how to read the room.

Cang Shubai put down his book and stood up. "Someone is coming."

Dr. Hu nimbly sat back in his rocking chair, crossed his legs, and said haughtily, "Little Cang, you’d better work hard, or I’ll deduct your wages!"

A man walked in.

His back was hunched, his head hung low, and he swayed with every step, his movements bizarre.

Dr. Hu realized something was wrong and sat up straight.

The man stumbled to the counter. "Doc... doc... doctor... I feel so terrible. I need... I need treatment. Please, help me... help me take a look."

Cang Shubai said, "You are not sick."

"Impossible! I am sick! I am sick!"

The man suddenly raised his head. His eyes were bloodshot, and his pale, bloodless face was covered in eerie black veins, which was terrifying to behold.

"Blood! Give me blood!"

The man stretched out his hands, his fingernails unnaturally long, and lunged at Cang Shubai. But the moment he met Cang Shubai’s eyes, he froze.

Those eyes had turned a cold, icy blue, like the deep sea, with faint blue specks of light that seemed capable of freezing even one’s breath.

"If you need blood, you should go outside and look for it."

The man blankly withdrew his hands. "I need to go outside and look... I need to go outside and look..."

He lowered his head again, hunched his back, turned around, and slowly walked out of the clinic.

Dr. Hu leaned in. "There’s a demonic cultivator using humans to cultivate a demonic beast!"

There had been rumors of a demonic cultivator killing people recently, but he hadn't expected one to actually show up in this remote little town.

Not long after, the startled cries of pedestrians echoed from outside.

Cang Shubai lowered his eyes and turned another page of the medical book, remaining indifferent to the surroundings.

Until, amidst the cries outside, a familiar voice reached his ears.

Dr. Hu felt a gust of wind, and Cang Shubai was already gone.

A man in coarse cloth fell to the ground in terror, facing the mutated man, who had opened his blood-stained maw toward him.

A small wooden ball was thrown, landing on the beast-like man and exploding into a flower of light, forcing him back a few steps.

But the blood-soaked man quickly steadied himself. He raised his red eyes, tilted his head, and headed straight for the woman who had meddled in his affairs.

Mu Ran was just about to turn and run when someone grabbed her hand and pulled her into a familiar embrace.

Cang Shubai lifted his icy eyes, his killing intent no longer hidden.

Just as the cold fish in his sleeve grew restless, a long sword flew through the air, piercing the body of the half-man, half-beast. The creature spat out a mouthful of blood and collapsed to the ground.

The next moment, the blood that fell to the ground bloomed into clusters of red spider lilies. The man's corpse was quickly swallowed by the flowers, creating a bizarre and bloody aesthetic.

The surrounding crowd gasped in shock.

The long sword flew back into the air, crossed over the crowd, and returned to the scabbard on the back of a blue-robed Taoist priest. The priest walked over, squatted down to look at the brilliantly blooming spider lilies, and said, "Another crooked path of demons."

The priest looked at the man who had fallen to the ground. "Are you alright?"

The man came to his senses, scrambled up to offer his thanks, then turned to bow to Mu Ran. "Mistress Mu, thank you for your help."

Mu Ran smiled. "Uncle Wang, you don't need to be so polite. I didn't really do much."

This man was their neighbor, Aunt Wang’s husband.

Uncle Wang was still shaken after his brush with death, but the world was in turmoil, and demons were not uncommon.

Moreover, he had errands to run. He said with a pale face that he would definitely invite Mu Ran and Cang Shubai to dinner another day, thanked the priest again, and ran off with shaky legs.

Only then did Mu Ran feel a low pressure.

She felt inexplicably nervous. She lifted her face and saw Cang Shubai’s expressionless features.

Cang Shubai rarely showed his emotions, and even now, one couldn't tell he was angry, yet she felt it nonetheless.

He said, "Acting rashly—are you looking to die?"

Mu Ran’s scalp tingled. "I know it was dangerous, but I couldn't help it."

"Are the lives of others more important than your own?"

Mu Ran lowered her head, pursed her lips, and whispered, "I just thought, if the person in danger today were Jinzhi, and no one stepped in to help, how helpless would Jinzhi be?"

Cang Shubai’s long eyelashes trembled.

He had tasted that helplessness for countless years; naturally, no one knew it better than he did.

She quietly lifted her eyes to look at him again. "And if Jinzhi couldn't come home, what would I do?"

Cang Shubai’s fingers, hanging at his side, curled imperceptibly. Finally, he reached out, brushed a stray lock of hair from her temple, and said softly, "What a silly goose."

chapters.title: I Miss You Too
chapters.content:
The Taoist priest crouched before the corpse, observing the blood-red flowers blooming upon it and the crimson patterns etched into its flesh. His brow furrowed deeper.

Someone in the crowd, seemingly well-informed, recognized the priest’s attire. "That’s a disciple from Chongyang Mountain!"

Chongyang Mountain was the nearest cultivation sect to the town. To the townspeople, it was a sacred mountain, and those who practiced there were, naturally, immortals.

The young priest stood up and looked toward Mu Ran, his gaze filled with curiosity. He walked over, first cupping his hands in a polite salute, and then said, "I just saw what you threw, young lady. It landed on the walking corpse and caused significant damage. You do not appear to be a cultivator, nor do you possess spiritual power. May I ask how you managed to command such a magical artifact?"

Cang Shubai stepped forward, blocking Mu Ran from view. "The priest is joking. That was merely a small trinket for self-defense, sold at the Song family workshop; it hardly qualifies as a magical artifact. If not for your intervention just now, my wife would likely have been caught up in the danger."

The priest sensed Cang Shubai’s aloofness.

This town lacked spiritual energy and had no cultivators. Among ordinary people, while some envied the cultivators who could tread the heavens and attain immortality, others naturally harbored a repulsion toward them, preferring not to interact with them too much.

However, this young man in green robes possessed an extraordinary air, quite different from the common folk.

The priest had important matters to attend to and could not afford to delay. Not wishing to make things difficult for others, he simply said, "My apologies for the intrusion."

Just as the gathered crowd had dispersed, the priest came and went.

The yamen officials arrived belatedly. Looking at the corpse on the ground, the most they could do was collect the body; they were powerless to handle anything else.

This world was like this—the strong preyed upon the weak. Who knew when two cultivators might destroy an entire city just to fight over resources?

This town was very remote and had originally been peaceful. For some reason, many cultivators had suddenly appeared recently. With a storm clearly brewing, the common folk only hoped that when the immortals fought, they wouldn't be the ones caught in the crossfire.

Cang Shubai held Mu Ran’s hand and led her into the medical clinic.

She had an abrasion on her hand from when she threw the small wooden ball; the explosion had grazed the skin on her palm. It wasn't serious, but Cang Shubai wouldn't let it slide easily.

Mu Ran sat on a chair, her hand resting obediently on the table, letting the young man carefully clean the wound with a cloth. His movements were gentle, causing her no pain, before he took out medicinal powder and lightly applied it to the scratch.

Cang Shubai remained silent throughout.

Mu Ran felt restless, afraid he was overthinking things and worried he might be angry.

She cast a pleading look toward the clinic owner nearby.

Boss Hu suddenly stood up from his recliner and paced about, saying, "Oh my, I'm hungry. I heard the restaurant has new dishes; I must go try them. Anyway, Little Cang, you stay here and watch the shop."

Without waiting for a reply from his subordinate, Boss Hu hurried out of the clinic, disappearing from sight in an instant.

With only the two of them left in the large clinic, Mu Ran felt her scalp tingle.

"Jinzhi, my dear Jinzhi, I know I was wrong. Please don't be angry, okay?"

Cang Shubai didn't speak. After applying the medicine to her wound, he took a white cloth strip to bandage it.

Mu Ran remembered when she first got together with him; he hadn't been very talkative, and she was the one who constantly pestered him to speak. Gradually, he began to talk more.

But at certain times, he would revert to being that silent, stubborn man.

Mu Ran moved her stool closer to him and tilted her head up, her sparkling eyes blinking like they held stars.

"Jinzhi, you promised me that no matter what, you wouldn't refuse to talk to me. If you don't talk and I don't talk, we won't know what the other is thinking. Relying solely on guessing is very exhausting, you know."

Cang Shubai finally finished bandaging her wound. His gaze shifted slightly, landing on her beautiful face. "No one's life is more important than your own."

"Not even yours, Jinzhi?"

He said, "No."

Mu Ran pursed her lips, clearly disagreeing with him.

Cang Shubai poured a cup of warm tea and brought it to her lips. "You said I couldn't refuse to talk. If you have something to say, just say it."

Mu Ran took a sip of water from the cup he offered to moisten her throat, then said, "It's unfair for you to demand something of me that you cannot do yourself."

Cang Shubai drank the remaining tea in the cup, his tone rising slightly. "How is it unfair?"

"In your eyes, whose life is more important—yours or mine?"

He answered without hesitation, "Yours."

"See? You don't even put your own life first, so why should I put mine first?" Mu Ran shook her head. "Do not impose on others what you yourself do not desire. Jinzhi, you are an educated man; how can you not understand this principle?"

Cang Shubai said, "You are afraid of pain. When it hurts badly, you cry in secret."

Mu Ran was left speechless.

Cang Shubai said every word clearly, "I will protect you well, and you must learn to protect yourself."

This world was too dangerous. There were far too many people who wanted to find a quiet corner to live in, only to have things turn out the opposite of their wishes. He had experienced countless bloody storms and knew deeply how fragile life was.

If those other people died, so be it.

But she was different.

Yet, she wasn't selfish enough; she was out of place in this world.

Every few days, Mu Ran had to endure Cang Shubai’s theory of "protecting yourself well," as if she were made of glass and would shatter at any moment.

Sometimes, she felt a bit unconvinced.

Mu Ran muttered, "Maybe one day you'll have to rely on me for protection."

Cang Shubai held her hands, wrapping them carefully until they were both warm. He said, "Ranran, I only wish for you to be safe and sound."

"Alright, alright, we will both be safe and sound." Mu Ran looked up and smiled, her eyes and lips curving into crescents. "I was reckless today. My dear Jinzhi, please don't scold me anymore. I was thinking of you the moment you left the house today."

She had always been clever and knew exactly what expression to use to make his heart soften.

A touch of tenderness appeared in Cang Shubai’s eyes. "There aren't many patients today. In half an hour, I will go home with you."

Mu Ran thought to herself, this clinic never has many patients; how does Boss Hu keep this place running? Doesn't he lose money?

Cang Shubai brought her some snacks to pass the time.

He still had to go count the medicinal herbs. Just as he stood up, he remembered something and asked, "Why did you come to town instead of sleeping in at home?"

Mu Ran’s hand, holding a sunflower seed, paused.

Cang Shubai was still staring at her.

Mu Ran felt the pressure mounting. Finally, she put down the seeds, wiped her hands, and seeing that no one was coming in, she cleared her throat and reached out her arms toward him.

"Jinzhi, I missed you."

Cang Shubai stood tall and graceful, remaining motionless for a long while.

She knew her excuse was clumsy; he must be suspicious!

Her arms were getting sore, and just as she was about to give up, the young man finally leaned over and took the initiative to let her embrace him.

He kissed the top of her hair and said, "I miss you too."

chapters.title: Blown Up
chapters.content:
Although Mu Ran sometimes had complaints about Boss Hu sending her husband up the mountain to gather herbs in the middle of the night, at other times, she felt that this boss was actually quite decent.

Just past the Shen hour today, Boss Hu said there were no customers and they should close early, which meant Cang Shubai could finish work ahead of schedule.

Since it was still early, Cang Shubai took Mu Ran for a stroll around town. However, even though he handed over all his wages to her, Mu Ran was very restrained when it came to spending money.

She bought a bag of warm mung bean cakes, placed them in Cang Shubai’s hands, and then smiled, "Let’s go home."

Cang Shubai reached out to smooth the hair on her forehead. "Don't you want to buy anything else?"

Mu Ran shook her head. "There’s nothing else I want."

He asked, "Something to eat, something to play with, clothes, jewelry, or perhaps a storybook?"

Mu Ran looked conflicted, then shook her head firmly. "No, no, I don't want any of it."

Cang Shubai nodded. "Alright, then let's go home."

Mu Ran held onto the jade pendant at his waist, following him forward. Hearing the lively hawking from all directions, she couldn't help but let her eyes wander.

That hairpin was so exquisite.That sugar figurine was made so cutely.And the green ru-skirt hanging in the clothing store was so pretty, too.

Cang Shubai stopped and looked down at her. "Are you really not buying anything?"

Mu Ran pursed her lips tightly, her brows furrowed. Her pretty face was scrunched up like a bun from the struggle; this conflicted expression was truly pitiful.

Cang Shubai was not in a hurry; he waited silently with great patience.

Finally, Mu Ran finished her internal struggle. She felt a bit embarrassed, her eyes curving into crescents. "Let's just buy one small thing."

Cang Shubai’s lips moved slightly. "Alright."

Mu Ran was very organized when it came to money and kept her own ledger. If she spent more than the budget in a month, she would become quite anxious.

She pondered in her heart how much surplus money she had for the month, her gaze shifting between several storefronts, before finally making a decision.

"Let's go to the bookstore!"

Cang Shubai sighed slightly.

When Mu Ran entered the bookstore, many customers were discussing the most popular books of the moment.

"Hey, the second volume of *The Amorous History of the Green-Clad Guest* is out. Have you read it?"

"Not yet, what happened? Tell me quickly, how many more beauties has the Green-Clad Guest taken in?"

"This time, the Green-Clad Guest took in the Red Ling Fairy. The two of them practiced dual cultivation for seven days and seven nights, tossing and turning, oblivious to the world—it was quite scandalous!"

"That’s not right, isn't the Red Ling Fairy an enemy of the Green-Clad Guest? The Green-Clad Guest killed people to seize treasures, and the Red Ling Fairy was no match for him. Her state of mind was affected, her path of cultivation was no longer smooth, and her progress stalled. She views him as a mortal enemy, so how could she possibly dual cultivate with him?"

"You don't understand, do you? Turning love into hate and finally submitting beneath the Green-Clad Guest is even more exciting!"

Someone else whispered, "Doesn't the name of this Red Ling Fairy in the story sound a lot like the Red Fu Fairy from the Red Flame Peak?"

"You don't know? This story of the Green-Clad Guest and the Red Ling Fairy is based on a battle between the Green-Clad Guest and the Red Fu Fairy in the Void Secret Realm two hundred years ago. The arrogant and exceptionally talented Red Fu Fairy lost to an unknown Green-Clad Guest. She hasn't had a breakthrough in her cultivation realm for years—it’s quite the topic of gossip."

Listening to the gossip, Mu Ran couldn't help but walk to the bookshelf. She secretly glanced at Cang Shubai, who was browsing other books, and quickly grabbed a copy of the newly released *The Amorous History of the Green-Clad Guest*.

The name alone sounded improper; it would surely be perfect for reading secretly in the middle of the night.

Mu Ran hid it and went to pay. Before she could even take it out, the book was snatched from her hands. Her hands were empty, and when she turned around, Cang Shubai was standing behind her, silent and still, watching her quietly. The pressure she felt was immense.

Mu Ran had always liked reading storybooks, especially those with "colorful" content, and she couldn't help but flip through them.

Cang Shubai didn't stop this little hobby of hers; sometimes he would even flip through them with her and then practice with her to see if the content in the books was feasible.

Thus, Mu Ran felt that her upright and honorable husband was actually a bit of a closet pervert.

She couldn't help but glance at the book in his hand. "Jinzhi, I didn't mean anything else, I just felt that we don't have enough books at home to read."

Cang Shubai said, "Not this one."

She was puzzled. "Why?"

"The content fabricated in this book is unrealistic."

Mu Ran glanced at the books in the hands of other customers. "But I see everyone likes reading it."

Cang Shubai put the book back, his tone indifferent. "Buy something else."

Mu Ran said "Oh," thinking to herself that her husband was a gentleman and perhaps couldn't stand to see the Red Fu Fairy from two hundred years ago being slandered with yellow rumors.

In the end, she picked up *A Few Things About the Sword Immortal and His Master's Wife* and paid for it before leaving.

As they stepped out of the bookstore, Cang Shubai asked the owner, "Which bookstore sent over that book about the Green-Clad Guest?"

The owner was busy calculating accounts and said offhandedly, "It was sent over from Wufang City."

Mu Ran was already standing on the street and turned back, asking suspiciously, "Jinzhi, what's wrong?"

Cang Shubai walked out of the bookstore, picked up the things in her hand, and took her hand. "I was thinking about what to eat tonight."

"The radishes we planted in the field should be grown by now. I want to have radish and pork rib soup today, okay?"

He said, "Alright."

"And there are still two fish you caught from the river in the water vat. Let’s cook one; I want to have boiled fish, okay?"

He nodded. "Alright."

"Hmm... I also want fish cakes and radish balls."

He said softly again, "Alright."

Cang Shubai’s temper was truly too good. Mu Ran made request after request, and he never found it troublesome, to the point where Mu Ran felt that if she said she wanted to see him perform swallowing a sword, he would do it without hesitation.

Mu Ran looked up at him. When they reached a secluded spot, she stood on tiptoe. Because he was much taller than her, it was a bit difficult, and he had to lean down to accommodate her.

She whispered deliberately into his ear, "Jinzhi, I want to eat you, is that okay?"

The young man’s eyes were deep, his fingers brushing over the ribbon on her dress. "Just don't regret it."

Mu Ran: "..."

She was already starting to regret it now. What should she do?

But facts proved that there was no such thing as a regret pill in this world.

The next day, Mu Ran lay in bed like a corpse, only opening her eyes hazily when the sun was high in the sky. When she moved her body, she felt sore everywhere.

Even eating ten meals of radish balls and fish cakes wouldn't make up for it!

Just as she turned over, she was pulled into the arms of the person who was also lazing in bed.

Mu Ran raised her eyes and caught sight of the scratch marks on his neck. Feeling slightly guilty, she shifted her body, lay in his arms, and played with his hair. "Don't you have to go to work today?"

"Boss Hu said I could go in later today."

When did he say that? Why hadn't she heard it?

Outside the window came the chirping of birds, and faintly, the gossip from the neighbors drifted in.

"Have you heard? The bookstore in Wufang City was blown up in the middle of the night!"

"What? Blown up?"

"Isn't that right? All the books there were blown to bits. What a pity!"

Mu Ran regained some energy and wanted to get up to join the gossip squad, but the hand resting on her waist held her with a firm, unyielding grip. She couldn't move.

Since she couldn't move, she gave up the idea and obediently lay back down.

The Green-Clad Guest.

Mu Ran silently repeated these three words in her heart and glanced at the clothes scattered messily on the floor. Her husband's green robe was very conspicuous beneath her beautiful pink skirt.

She raised her head and stared straight at her husband's handsome face.

Cang Shubai opened his eyes, the corners of his eyes slightly curved, still revealing a hint of fatigue and laziness. "What is it?"

"Jinzhi, you wouldn't happen to be that Green-Clad Guest, would you?"

Before Cang Shubai could deny it, Mu Ran laughed out loud, cupping his face.

"You spent so much energy last night, where would you have the strength to go blow up someone's bookstore?"

She rested peacefully back on his chest and closed her eyes to take a nap.

After a long while, the man's large hand gently stroked her cheek. In her comfort and drowsiness, she seemed to hear a soft...

chapters.title: The Ends of the Earth
chapters.content:
"Fairy Hongfu, this is a little trinket we stumbled upon. We thought it was rather interesting, so we came specifically to present it for your amusement."

Two young men, wearing fawning smiles, respectfully presented a small wooden box.

A maid took the box and walked back, delivering it to the woman in red.

Hongfu sat in her chair and glanced at the small wooden box.

The maid understood and opened the box, revealing a chubby little wooden chicken inside.

Hongfu asked, "What is this?"

The two men stepped forward to demonstrate. One of them fed a strand of his hair to the chicken and spoke a sentence. Although the wooden chicken looked plump, it flapped its wings and flew over to the other man, repeating the sentence it had just received word for word.

One maid remarked, "Isn't this just like a sound-transmission talisman? What is there to be so rare about?"

The slightly taller man replied, "The young lady is mistaken. A sound-transmission talisman requires both parties to carry identical talisman paper to communicate. But this wooden chicken, as long as it has a strand of hair from a person, can locate that person within a hundred-mile radius and then transmit the message."

The shorter man added, "So, this wooden chicken can not only transmit messages but also track people."

The two maids exchanged glances, vaguely sensing the value of this little gadget.

Hongfu also became interested. She reached out, and the wooden chicken flew onto her palm. She asked, "What is this thing called?"

One man replied, "This object is called a 'Paging Chicken'."

Hongfu said, "The name is quite fitting."

Although she wore a veil that obscured her face, Fairy Hongfu possessed skin like jade and bones like ivory. A slender, flawless wrist hung gracefully from her wide sleeve. Her eyes, visible above the veil, shimmered like autumn water, and as her lashes fluttered, they carried a touch of ethereal coldness, as if she were untainted by the mortal world.

Those who saw her felt that even without seeing her full face, this glimpse of her celestial grace was enough to enchant the three realms.

The two men could not help but let their minds wander, but when Hongfu’s gaze swept over them, they felt a jolt of alarm and quickly lowered their heads, not daring to look further.

Hongfu was satisfied enough with the gift. She had the maid take the Paging Chicken and asked lazily, "Speak, what is it you seek?"

The two men hurriedly said:

"Our status is humble; we dare not ask anything of you, Fairy."

"It is just that we are no longer young, and suffering from the lack of a sect, our cultivation has remained stagnant."

"We heard that Chiyan Peak is recruiting disciples recently, but without a recommendation, we don't even have the qualifications to ascend the mountain."

Both men wore troubled expressions, looking pitifully at the immortal before them.

Hongfu chuckled, "Ascending Chiyan Peak is not difficult, but whether you can be selected depends on your own fortune."

The maid took out two rings and placed them into the hands of the two men; these were equivalent to tokens for entering Chiyan Peak.

The two men were overjoyed, clutching the tokens and thanking her profusely. Not daring to linger and disturb the fickle Fairy Hongfu, they left in a hurry, nearly colliding with a young Taoist priest on their way out.

It was no secret that Hongfu was staying at the inn, and many minor cultivators hoped to curry favor and gain some benefits. However, this Taoist priest was different.

"Yue Qingfeng, a disciple of Chongyang Mountain, pays his respects to Martial Aunt Hongfu."

Chiyan Peak and Chongyang Mountain had always maintained good relations. Hongfu was of the same generation as Yue Qingfeng’s master, so it was appropriate for him to address her as Martial Aunt.

Yue Qingfeng kept his head lowered and said, "My master heard that Martial Aunt Hongfu was coming to capture the Elder of the Long Sword, so he specifically ordered me to come and assist.
